## p_3263884 : 2020-03-17_fiche_de_synthese_troubles_du_neurodeveloppement_en_relmd_modif_acceptees

Neurodevelopmental disorders
Detection and referral of at-risk children
February 2020
OBJECTIVES
The aims of this guideline are to:
■ harmonise detection and referral practices in children with a neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) in an at-risk population from birth to 7 years of age (7 years and 11 months) within formalised paediatric care networks and by primary healthcare professionals in conjunction with them;
■ optimise the pathway of the child and his/her family, from identification of warning signs of NDD through to referral for early intervention and/or to a second-line diagnostic and management team.
NDDs1 begin during the development period and include:
■ intellectual disabilities (intellectual development disorder);
■ communication disorders;
■ autism spectrum disorder;
■ specific learning disorder (reading, written expression and dyscalculia);
■ motor disorders (developmental coordination disorder, stereotypies, tics);
■ attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD);
■ other NDDs, specified (for example, NDD associated with prenatal alcohol exposure), or otherwise.
  NDD RISK FACTORS
High NDD risk factors
■ Very premature birth (< 32 weeks [GA or gestational age]) (grade B).
■ Premature birth < 37 weeks GA with intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR) or small for gestational age (SGA)
< 3rd percentile or < - 2 SD for GA and gender according to national reference growth charts (grade B).
■ Encephalopathy presumed to be hypoxic-ischemic with an indication of therapeutic hypothermia (grade B).
1. DSM 5 – Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of mental disorders – American Psychiatric Association.
QUICK REFERENCE GUIDE

■ A perinatal arterial stroke (diagnosed between the 20th week of foetal life and the 28th day of life; including in premature neonates) (grade B).
■ Brain growth abnormalities: microcephaly with head circumference < - 2 SD at birth, verified subsequently (grade C) or macrocephaly > + 3 SD for the term (EC) (persisting after a second measurement).
■ Family history of severe NDD in a first-degree relative (brother, sister or parent) (grade C).
■ Symptomatic congenital cytomegalovirus infection (grade C) and other infectious foetal diseases: toxoplasmosis, Zika, rubella, etc.
■ Bacterial and herpes virus-induced meningoencephalitis (grade C).
■ Surgically-treated complex congenital heart diseases (grade C):
● transposition of the great arteries;
● hypoplastic left heart syndrome.
■ Prenatal exposure to a major toxin:
● certain anti-epileptic drugs (sodium valproate) (grade B);
● severe alcohol exposure and/or with signs of foetal disease (grade B).
■ Major, prolonged and repeated surgery (heart, brain, abdominal, thoracic) (EC).
Moderate NDD risk factors
■ Moderate prematurity at 32 weeks GA + 0 days to 33 weeks GA + 6 days (grade B).
■ Late prematurity at 34 weeks GA + 0 days to 36 weeks GA + 6 days (grade B).
■ Small for gestational age (SGA): < 3rd percentile or < - 2 SD for GA and gender according to national reference growth charts (grade B).
■ Cerebral or cerebellar malformations of undetermined prognosis (isolated corpus callosum agenesis or dysgenesis, ventriculomegaly > 15 mm, small cerebellum with or without cerebellar vermis abnormality, cystic malformations of the posterior fossa) (grade C).
■ Grade 1 encephalopathy presumed to be hypoxic-ischemic (grade C).
■ Significant alcohol exposure without signs of foetal disease (EC).
■ Prenatal exposure to a psychoactive substance (psychotropic drugs, illegal substances) (grade C).
■ Septic shock with positive blood cultures (grade C).
■ Enteroviral meningoencephalitis (EC).
The child’s environment may suggest circumstances to be taken into consideration, particularly the family environment, some impacts of which can place the child in the high NDD risk category (EC). These are:
■ high level of socio-economic vulnerability: no fixed address, below the poverty threshold, isolated parent, low level of education of parents, etc.;
■ psycho-affective vulnerability: marital/domestic violence, history of negative life experiences of the mother, exposure of the child to serious abuse or negligence, current psychological or psychiatric difficulties in the family environment, etc.
  REFERRAL ON THE BASIS OF NDD RISK FACTORS
The identification of any risk factors should ideally be carried out during the prenatal period (hence the importance of the pre-conception consultation by the primary care physician and the consultation at the 4th month of pregnancy) or the perinatal period. Otherwise, it is necessary to remember to look for these factors in the presence of a child with warning signs or clinical red flags for NDD. (EC)
It is recommended that children with a moderate NDD risk factor have screening consultations with a first-line physician. The latter may be the doctor who provides the child’s regular care (general practitioner or paediatrician), a doctor in maternal and child protection centre (PMI) or the school doctor. (EC)
It is recommended that children with a high risk factor for NDD leave the neonatal department with an appointment for a specialised neurodevelopment consultation with a reference physician specifically trained in NDDs, in either a hospital or private practitioner, particularly one affiliated to a follow-up network and/or second-line structure.

IDENTIFICATION OF NDD SIGNS
Red flags
Red flags are developmental delays compared to the general population using the development tables in the child’s personal health record. A check for red flags is recommended as part of the medical examination carried out during each mandatory health check-up, correcting the age of preterm babies on the basis of their gestational age at birth, up until the chronological age of 2 years.
This investigation should be conducted by the doctor who provides the child’s regular care, or by the PMI doctor or the school doctor as part of routine visits carried out at school.
Irrespective of the child’s age, any parental concern about their child’s neurodevelopment should be considered to be a red flag (EC). The same is true for any developmental regression or non-progression. (EC)
Warning signs
Warning signs correspond to a significant deviation from the developmental trajectory and require rapid referral for diagnosis.
FIRST-LINE SCREENING CONSULTATION
In children at moderate risk of NDD, developmental discrepancies are specified and documented during a screening consultation performed by the first-line doctor. (EC)
■ This consultation must be dedicated to screening, be sufficiently long and not be connected with other care or follow-up objectives.
■ During this consultation, the doctor will conduct a comprehensive clinical assessment and will look for warning signs of NDD in accordance with the French interministerial delegation for autism and neurodevelopmental disorders’ table for Detection of unusual development in children under the age of 7 years2.
■ The warning signs should be looked for on the basis of the child’s chronological age (actual age based on birth date) or corrected age compared to full term (40 weeks GA) in babies born prematurely (< 37 weeks GA) up to the age of 2 years.
■ When several NDD warning signs are detected during the first-line consultation, both an early intervention (see below) and referral for a specialised neurodevelopmental consultation or to the ASD/NDD coordination and referral platform where this exists3 are recommended. (EC)
  SPECIALISED NEURODEVELOPMENTAL CONSULTATION
In children at high risk of NDD, it is recommended to look for warning signs during a specialised neurodevelopmental consultation conducted by a doctor trained in NDDs from the outset.
The objective of the specialised neurodevelopmental consultation is to confirm or eliminate a developmental trajectory deviation and determine whether or not this deviation is pathological. It is not a substitute for a multidisciplinary specialised diagnosis (EC). It will consist of:
■ an assessment including:
● gross and fine motor skills, and coordination,
● speech, language, social engagement, self-control and control of activities, and working memory,
● observation of spontaneous and triggered behaviour,
● school learning,
● verification of completion of standard screening tests (hearing, vision);
2. www.handicap.gouv.fr/plateformes-TND
3. The criteria for referral to the platform in accordance with the French interministerial delegation for autism and neurodevelopmental disorders’ table for Detection of unusual development in children under the age of 7 years (annex 1) are as follows:
- for children aged 0 to 3 years: 2 signs in at least 2 of the 4 development areas;
- for children aged 4 to 6 years: 3 signs in at least 2 of the 5 development areas.
The development areas are: gross motor skills, postural control and locomotion; fine motor skills; language; socialisation; cognition
(from 4 years of age).

■ the proposal of validated standardised screening tests as a function of assessment results (see Screening tests box);
■ a complete clinical paediatric assessment (weight, height, head circumference, general physical examination, etc.).
The consultation should make it possible to position the child with respect to standard typical development in the different areas of functioning assessed (Denver scale, WHO neuromotor skills scale).
  REFERRAL BASED ON THE RESULTS OF THE SPECIALISED
  NEURODEVELOPMENT CONSULTATION
■ If a neurodevelopmental disorder is strongly suspected at this consultation (figure 1):
● It is necessary to refer the child as soon as possible, depending on the disorder detected and the priority objective determined, for early interventions (assessment adapted to the symptoms and early rehabilitative therapy if necessary). (Table 1) (EC). Where these exist in the area, the child may benefit from early care packages in the context of ASD/NDD coordination and referral platforms.
● The expected time between the detection of developmental abnormalities and the start of interventions should be less than 3 months in children under the age of 18 months and 6 months beyond this age. (EC)
● In the event of severe NDD affecting several areas of functioning, or in the absence of any improvement following 3 months of well-conducted interventions, a specialised NDD diagnostic consultation should be scheduled with a specialised multidisciplinary team. (EC)
● In all cases and pending the implementation of early interventions, it is also recommended to provide patients with advice and put in place parental guidance (see below) to initiate activities at home, and to systematically propose socialisation of young children in a multi-care setting. (EC)
■ In the event of doubt concerning the results of the specialised neurodevelopmental consultation, particularly if it does not confirm the concerns raised by the parents or the doctor providing the child’s regular care, the child should undergo another clinical assessment 3 months later. A new screening test, appropriate to age and the disorder suspected, may be proposed. (EC)
■ If no NDD is suspected at the specialised neurodevelopmental consultation, continued monitoring of the child’s development via the child’s usual medical follow-up is recommended, in particular at the recommended check-ups from birth to 7 years. (EC)
Screening tests
Tests do not replace a clinical expert assessment. They are useful to structure the clinical assessment. They must be interpreted in the light of the clinical assessment and will guide decisions for referral for early interventions and/or multidisciplinary diagnostic consultations.
■ In children at high risk of NDD, it is recommended to systematically use a standardised overall screening test at the ages of 9, 18, 24, 30-36 months and 4, 5 years (see figure 2 and Annex 2 of the guideline). (EC)
■ In the event of parental concerns or concerns expressed by staff working in the early childhood sector (regular or drop-in childcare centre, school, etc.), or medical concerns, an age-appropriate standardised overall NDD screening test may be used outside the ages recommended above. (EC)
■ Standardised specific screening tests should be used to explore the area(s) in which the child failed the overall screening test (see Figure 2 and Annex 2 of the guideline).
■ In the event of doubt concerning social communication or behavioural disorders and restricted interests, it is recommended to use a specific ASD screening test at 18 and 24 months and also at any visit, as a function of age. (EC)
■ Contact with the school is recommended to obtain objective feedback with respect to school learning. From the time the child starts school, their school trajectory is included in the NDD assessment. (EC)

EARLY INTERVENTIONS
In children at risk of NDD, these interventions must be implemented as early as possible, from the hospitalisation period or when they leave the neonatal unit, during the first year of life. (EC)
■ In children at risk of NDD, it is recommended that early preventive interventions be initiated from the neonatal period in hospital (developmental care) and be continued once the child returns home (mobile teams, HAH), to avoid any interruption of care. (EC)
■ In children in whom NDD is strongly suspected on the basis of the clinical assessment and screening tests, it is recommended that parental guidance be put in place and that educational and rehabilitative interventions be prescribed as soon as possible (Table 1) (grade C). It is recommended that the child be referred to a paramedical professional and/or psychologist trained in paediatric neurodevelopment. (EC)
Table 1. Table for referral to early interventions, simultaneously or pending diagnosis (EC)

Parental guidance
It is essential to value parents’ feelings of competence and to make them central to their child's care and education. Neonates at risk of NDD may present difficulties regulating their emotions, which may impair the quality of interactions with their family. It is recommended that strategies to assist and support the development of these emotional regulation skills be incorporated in the intervention and training programmes usually offered to the parents of vulnerable “at risk” children at a very early stage. (EC)

PATHWAY FOR CHILDREN AT RISK OF NDD AND THEIR FAMILIES
Figure 1. Diagram of the pathway of a child (0 to 7 years) at risk of NDD
Medical follow-up and reassessment
The detection of a neurodevelopmental disorder does not dispense with the need for regular medical follow-up of children by their primary care physician (general practitioner or paediatrician), or the doctor from the maternal and child protection centre (PMI) relative to the various dimensions of their health or their needs. (EC)
The child’s primary care physician detects NDD warning signs. This physician may initially be the reference doctor for NDD follow-up. (EC)
A doctor specifically trained in NDD will be the reference doctor from the outset if the child is at high risk of NDD or subsequently if the child’s condition becomes more complex (EC). In these cases, this doctor ensures follow-up of the NDD and coordination of the child’s care in liaison with the parents and second-line teams and with the school. He/she will handle the administrative procedures (MDPH (regional centre for disability) and recognition of chronic condition if required. (EC)
It is recommended that the primary care physician be informed, with the parents’ agreement, about assessments conducted with respect to rehabilitation, socialisation, schooling and progress observed.
It is recommended that the reference physician should be able to consult liaison childcare professionals (childcare professionals from neonatal units, home care teams, early medical-social action centre (CAMSP) childcare professionals, maternal and child protection centre (PMI) to ensure parental guidance is provided, ideally at home, or otherwise via telephone or telemedicine procedures. (EC)
In the event of any aggravating factors due to a disadvantaged social situation, referral to a maternal and child protection centre (PMI) ) is recommended so that follow-up of the child’s health status and appropriate social measures can be put in place, in particular by means of home visits. (EC)

Socialisation and social integration
It is recommended that children at high risk of NDD or with a suspected NDD be put into an early-years childcare facility (drop-in and regular daycare centres, parent and baby groups) as soon as possible. (EC)
Inclusive school
It is recommended that a link be established, with the agreement of the parents (or the persons with parental authority), between the first-line doctor, the reference teacher and, if possible, school health professionals (doctor and/or nurse). (EC)
It is recommended that the reference doctor be able to advise families on the various types of school support that their child may benefit from. Parents are advised to contact the child’s school doctor to discuss measures tailored to the child. (EC)
It is recommended not to await a precise diagnosis before requesting schooling adaptations, if the child’s assessment indicates the need for such a request (for example in the case of an unspecified NDD). (EC)
Coordination between the different professionals
It is recommended that coordination between professionals be set up in order to link the care programme to the schooling programme. (EC)
  ANNOUNCEMENT OF NDD SCREENING RESULT AND INFORMING OF FAMILIES
Parents must be informed early on of the need for follow-up and organisation of this follow-up whenever a risk is detected in their child, from the hospitalisation period in the neonatal unit if applicable. (EC)
It is recommended that the family be involved in the detection process. (EC)
Announcement of the medical screening result is an ethical obligation. It is recommended that the result be announced in the presence of both parents if possible, at a dedicated diagnosis announcement consultation with the primary care physician and/or the reference doctor. (EC)
This information must be clear, honest and complete, but care should be taken to modulate the identified risk in a way that is clear to parents (do not cause excessive worry, but motivate parents to comply with risk-appropriate follow-up). It will explain the concept of risk factors, which require follow-up but do not predict the prognosis. (EC)
It must be repeated at each consultation and the discourse must be harmonised between the various professionals responsible for the child’s care. (EC)
To this end, the child’s personal health record (confidential document) should be the reference tool. Each healthcare professional who sees the child must note the risk factors identified in this record, during the neonatal period and during subsequent follow-up. (EC)
If risk factors are identified from the neonatal period, they must be the subject of a letter sent to the parents, with a copy to be given to the child’s doctor if the latter has not already been identified. (EC)
The essential notion to be outlined to parents when giving this information is that of a neurodevelopmental trajectory, which is not fixed at the end of the neonatal period, but which will progress on the basis of numerous parameters, in particular environmental stimulations that are beneficial or detrimental to the child’s development. (EC)
The value of reinforced follow-up must be explained to parents, stressing the fact that it is an identified risk, not a diagnosis: their child has not been identified as having a disorder but of being at risk of developing one. Reinforced follow-up will enable the child to be treated more rapidly if a disorder is identified and hence improve the prognosis. (EC)
It is recommended that parents be informed about the different steps in the future pathway and that the first follow-up appointment be made before they leave the neonatal unit, either with a primary care physician or a doctor from the network for the follow-up of children at risk of NDD. (EC) (cf. Referral on the basis of NDD risk factors)
If the parents are particularly anxious, in particular with respect to the situation, it is essential to take this into account; it may be proposed that parents contact family associations or consult a psychologist trained in neonatal conditions or neurodevelopmental disorders. (EC)
The importance of supporting families at home in the event of a high risk level or major vulnerability is reiterated. (EC)

  INFORMATION AND TRAINING OF PROFESSIONALS AND CARERS
It is recommended to (EC):
■ develop new communication tools (telemedicine, secure health messaging system) in order to facilitate dialogue between professionals, remote consultations and training of families and carers;
■ train first and second-line doctors in neurodevelopment and tools to monitor normal child development as well as in warning signs of NDD;
■ update the training of healthcare professionals concerning the pathway of the child and his/her family, from detection to diagnosis, in order to reduce the gap between the recommended practices and the practices actually implemented, which are sometimes far removed from the international guidelines;
■ train the various healthcare professionals in the use of screening tools;
■ circulate this information to other early-years medico-social and child protection professionals and school professionals, in order to raise their awareness of normal child development and the identification of warning signs;
■ promote interdisciplinary and inter-institutional training.
